title: Why Brand New Ships Are Already Covered in Rust
hook: Why is this ship rusting when it is barely a year old?
loop: Ends on 'which is why almost every working ship you will ever see' handing back into scene 2. Pattern A.

scenes.text: Look at almost any working ship, and you will see rust running down the sides in long streaks.
Some of these vessels left the shipyard less than a year ago.
So is the steel already failing? Did somebody simply stop maintaining it?
Most of that rust is not the hull at all.
A ship is covered in thousands of smaller parts. Railings, bolts, hatches, brackets, hinges.
They are made from different alloys, fitted by different hands, at different times.
And every one of them creates an edge, a seam, or a joint.
Salt water finds every single one.
It collects in the gaps, and out at sea it never fully dries.
Salt also holds moisture against the metal long after the spray has stopped.
So the small parts corrode first, long before the plating around them.
Water runs off each corroded fitting and carries the stain downward across perfectly good paint.
The streak is not damage. It is a trail left by something small, higher up.
Crews grind and repaint those fittings constantly, and the sea starts again immediately.
A spotless hull at sea does not mean a healthy ship. It usually means a very recent repaint.
Which is why almost every working ship you will ever see
